member.name: T:HumanGateway.Core.Convergence.ConvergenceAckPolicy
member.summary: The sender-side safe-acknowledgement rule for the durable outbox (SYNC-FR-04, SYNC-FR-06, NF-05). An outbox entry may be marked sent — and discarded from the durable outbox — only once the receiver's contiguous cursor covers its sequence. This is the complement to on the sender's side of the store-and-forward loop.

remarks.para: Marking an entry sent on any successful response, regardless of the receiver's cursor, can strand a sequence past a gap: if the sender discards entries the receiver has not contiguously acknowledged, a partial failure leaves a permanent hole that no retry can fill (the entry is gone, and the receiver never advances past the missing predecessor). Retaining everything past the contiguous cursor guarantees the next push re-sends the tail, so a gap is always fillable from the sender's side (SYNC-FR-06).

The receiver's cursor is opaque on the wire; the sender decodes its own issued position via before applying this policy. This policy is pure — it decides from the two numbers (entry sequence, receiver contiguous cursor) and carries no I/O.

member.name: T:HumanGateway.Core.Convergence.ConvergenceAnalyzer
member.summary: Pure, deterministic convergence analysis for a gateway's applied sequence stream (SYNC-FR-04, SYNC-FR-06). This is the long-disconnect / partial-failure primitive: given the full set of sequences a receiver has applied, it reports the contiguous cursor (reusing ), the applied high-watermark, and the exact missing ranges below it. The receiver is converged iff there are no such gaps.

remarks.para: Analysis is order-independent and idempotent: the same multiset of applied sequences always yields the same regardless of arrival order, and duplicates collapse. This makes the result safe to property-test by shuffling, and safe to recompute from a durable inbox that may contain replays.

The gap list is represented as closed ranges rather than an enumeration of individual sequences, so a pathological stream (e.g. applied {1, 1_000_000_000}) yields a single gap range instead of a billion-entry list. The number of ranges is bounded by the number of distinct applied sequences.

member.name: T:HumanGateway.Core.Delivery.DeliveryTransitioner
member.summary:
Performs delivery-state transitions on a (product vision §10, SYNC-FR-05). This is the deterministic, pure counterpart to : the state machine answers "is this transition legal?", while the transitioner performs it — stamping the state-entry timestamp, advancing the attempt counter where appropriate, and attaching failure details — and returns the next envelope. It never mutates its input.
Two entry points mirror the two sides of the store-and-forward contract:
drives the sender's own lifecycle: QUEUED → SYNCING → DELIVERED → ACKNOWLEDGED, with WAITING_FOR_SYNC for offline deferral and FAILED gated by the retry budget ().
consumes a delivery acknowledgement returned by the recipient (SYNC-FR-05): DELIVERED/ACKNOWLEDGED advance the sender's record, and FAILED marks a permanent recipient rejection (independent of the sender's retry budget).
Both are idempotent (at-least-once → exactly-once effect, NF-05): a replayed transition or a replayed ack that has already been satisfied has no further effect.

member.name: T:HumanGateway.Core.Idempotency.IdempotencyKeys
member.summary: Deterministic idempotency-key derivation (SYNC-FR-02). The key identifies a logical batch by durable identity — the batch ID plus each item's kind, sequence, and durable ID — not by payload bytes. A retry that re-sends the same items therefore derives the same key (so the receiver collapses it as a replay), while a change to the batch ID or to an item's durable identity yields a new logical batch. Payload integrity (tamper/change detection) is the content hash's job, verified separately (also SYNC-FR-02). The result is a sha256:<hex> hash, matching the schema's ^[A-Za-z0-9._:-]+$ shape.

member.name: T:HumanGateway.Core.Ordering.SequenceOrdering

remarks.para: Determinism is order-independent: the same multiset of items always reorders to the same sequence regardless of arrival order, so Reorder(shuffle(x)) == Reorder(x) for any permutation. This is a stronger guarantee than a plain stable sort, which would leak the arrival order into the result whenever two items share a sequence number (which must not happen per gateway, but can arrive when a retry overlaps, or when batches from distinct sources are merged).

Equal sequence numbers are therefore tie-broken by a stable payload identity derived from the item's durable ID (the message, delivery, artifact, or ack ID), never by input position. The result is a pure function of the item contents, which is what makes the reorder safe to property-test by shuffling.
